ANSWERED AT CYCLE 28 (T3), after ten cycles in which it was merely articulated. THE QUESTION WAS: did ENISA's APT29/'Midnight Blizzard' naming-convention hallucination (src-0004) contribute to, or correlate with, the kind of plausible-but-wrong attribution measured quantitatively in src-0002, or is it a distinct hallucination sub-type (citation/naming fabrication vs. attribution judgment)? THE ANSWER IS: DISTINCT SUB-TYPE. THE DECIDING ARGUMENT COMES FROM src-0002'S OWN SCORING RULE, already stored verbatim in this base: 'To further ensure accuracy, we manually verify each LLM response to account for the multiple aliases that threat actors often use.' CTI-TAA SCORES AN ALIAS AS CORRECT -- its 'correct answer' bucket is defined as 'when the LLM accurately identifies the threat actor or one of its aliases'. APT29 and Midnight Blizzard are two names for one group, and the ENISA passage names the right group; its error is the claim about WHICH VENDOR USES WHICH NAME, i.e. a false statement about naming provenance, not a false statement about who conducted the activity. Under CTI-TAA's own rule the ENISA sentence would be scored CORRECT. The ENISA defect is therefore INVISIBLE TO THE MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENT this issue's quantified leg rests on, and the two cannot be instances of one measured phenomenon. Two corroborating considerations, neither load-bearing: the same ENISA report's other documented defect is 26 of 492 incorrect footnotes, a citation-validity failure of exactly the kind src-0011 (GhostCite) and src-0012 (EY Canada) measure; and src-0004 attaches no accuracy or confidence measurement of any kind to the passage. CONSEQUENCE, RECORDED AGAINST THIS ISSUE'S OWN INTEREST: src-0004's evidential home is institutional-incident-real-world-impact, and it must not be counted as an independent second source for THIS issue's central claim -- which is why the primary candidate below now cites src-0002 alone, where it previously cited src-0002 and src-0004. RESIDUAL, GENUINELY OPEN AND NOT TO BE ASSERTED EITHER WAY: whether the two sub-types share an upstream generative cause (both being ungrounded production of a specific-looking fact) is a mechanism question that no source in this base tests.

candidate_resolutions.summary: REWRITTEN AT CYCLE 28 (T3), executing step (i) of ctr-0002's resolution path. THE 86-VS-52 FRAMING IS RETIRED, NOT REPAIRED. The old text of this candidate said 'every one of the 5 tested models' plausible-sounding attribution rate substantially exceeds its correct attribution rate (e.g. GPT-4-turbo: 86% plausible vs 52% correct; Gemini-1.5: 74% vs 38%)'; CTIBench defines Plausible Accuracy as 'the fraction of correct and plausible answers combined', so it CONTAINS Correct Accuracy and that inequality is true by construction for every model on every dataset. It evidenced nothing and is withdrawn. WHAT REPLACES IT. CTI-TAA partitions each response into three buckets, verbatim: 'correct answer (when the LLM accurately identifies the threat actor or one of its aliases), plausible answer (when the threat report lacks sufficient details to pinpoint the answer, but the LLM provides a plausible or related threat actor within a similar group), and incorrect answer (when the LLM misattributes the threat actor due to misjudgment, hallucination, or spurious correlation)'. The THIRD bucket is the paper's own hallucination-inclusive misattribution rate and equals 100 minus Plausible Accuracy: GPT-4-turbo 14%, GPT-3.5-turbo 38%, Gemini-1.5 26%, LLAMA3-70B 20%, LLAMA3-8B 64%, over 50 real threat reports, with the authors stating that they 'manually verify each LLM response to account for the multiple aliases that threat actors often use'. THOSE FIVE VALUES ARE DERIVED BY SUBTRACTION FROM TABLE 1 BY THIS AGENT AND ARE NOT PRINTED ANYWHERE IN THE PAPER; every cell they are derived from was re-verified EXACT against Table 1 by two independent fetches at cycle 23, and the ChatGPT-4 row was re-confirmed a third time at cycle 28. THE FINDING: outright misattribution of the threat actor is common in 2024-era models, from roughly one report in seven for the best model to nearly two in three for the weakest, on real reports scored with alias tolerance. WHAT THIS CANDIDATE DOES NOT CLAIM, and the distinction is the whole point of this issue: src-0002 measures WRONGNESS, NOT CONFIDENCE. It records no verbalised confidence, no hedging rate, no calibration metric and no reader-facing plausibility judgement, and no sentence in the paper interprets the correct-versus-plausible gap. Its 'plausible' bucket is scoped to UNDERDETERMINED INPUT answered with a related actor from a similar group -- arguably reasonable behaviour under ambiguity -- and is explicitly NOT its hallucination bucket. The string 'plausible-sounding' does not occur in the paper, though this state presented it in scare quotes for 27 cycles. This candidate is therefore supported as an ATTRIBUTION-ERROR-RATE finding and supplies no support whatever for the 'confident' half of this issue's title. src-0004 has been REMOVED from this candidate's evidence: see open_question[2], answered this cycle, which finds the ENISA error to be a distinct sub-type invisible to CTI-TAA's scoring rule.

issues.title: How confidently do LLMs assert threat-actor attributions they get wrong -- and is that quantity measured by anything at all?
open_questions: CREATED AT CYCLE 45 (T2) BY SPLITTING attribution-confident-wrong-gap, per carry-forward [45], which had requested the split since cycle 25. READ THAT ISSUE'S open_questions[3] FIRST -- it records the split in full, including why the OTHER issue kept the now-misleading legacy id 'attribution-confident-wrong-gap' (it is cited from three APPEND-ONLY knowledge files and cannot legally be renamed). THIS ISSUE IS THE LEG WITH NO EVIDENCE, AND THAT IS ITS ENTIRE POINT: it exists so that the well-evidenced attribution-ERROR-RATE leg can be scored on its own merits instead of being held down by a question nothing in this base answers, and so that the unanswered question stays VISIBLE instead of being quietly absorbed as a caveat on somebody else's number. A SUCCESSOR MUST NOT TREAT A LOW SCORE HERE AS A FINDING ABOUT THE WORLD. It is a finding about the evidence base.

THE PRIMARY OPEN QUESTION, AND IT IS A COLLECTION QUESTION BEFORE IT IS AN ANALYTIC ONE: does ANY published evaluation measure expressed confidence on threat-actor attribution -- verbalised confidence ('I am 80% sure'), token-level probability, hedging rate, refusal/abstention rate, or a calibration statistic such as ECE or Brier computed ON AN ATTRIBUTION TASK? NO SOURCE IN THIS BASE DOES, as of cycle 45 and as surveyed at cycle 28. THIS IS A T1 TARGET AND NO SCHEDULED TASK CURRENTLY REACHES IT. Note precisely what would and would not count: a calibration number on a DIFFERENT task set does NOT count (see the next question), and an accuracy or error rate does NOT count at any exchange rate, because a model can be uniformly wrong while being uniformly hedged or uniformly strident and the error rate cannot distinguish those cases.

WHY THE NEAREST-LOOKING EVIDENCE DOES NOT TRANSFER, RECORDED SO NOBODY RE-DISCOVERS IT AND SO NOBODY IMPORTS IT ANYWAY. The base DOES contain confidence and calibration measurements -- src-0001's and src-0013's ECE and Brier scores -- but they are computed on ENTIRELY DIFFERENT TASK SETS and belong to consistency-calibration-as-failure-mode, which is listed in this issue's depends_on for exactly that reason. The genuinely open question is whether calibration behaviour measured on those tasks TRANSFERS to attribution, and NOTHING IN THIS BASE TESTS TRANSFER. Until something does, importing an ECE from another task to stand in for attribution confidence would be an operationalisation mismatch of the shape this project has already booked twice. THE THREE SOURCES CLOSEST TO THIS ISSUE ALL FAIL IT FOR STATED REASONS: src-0002 partitions CTI-TAA outputs by CORRECTNESS ONLY (correct / plausible / incorrect) and records no confidence construct of any kind, and its 'plausible' bucket is scoped to UNDERDETERMINED INPUT answered with a related actor from a similar group -- arguably reasonable behaviour under ambiguity, and NOT a confidence measurement; src-0007's 'Content: Threat Actor' block is an LLM-judged 1-5 QUALITY rubric whose absolute level is uninterpretable and which, per ctr-0008, measures SOURCE LINKING rather than actor identification in its 'Attribution' row; src-0004 is a single published passage with no measurement attached at all. Also note, from src-0002's own text, that the exact string 'plausible-sounding' DOES NOT OCCUR IN THE PAPER, though this project presented it in scare quotes as a quotation for 27 cycles -- the phrase in this issue's ancestry is OURS, not a source's.

A DESIGN QUESTION THIS ISSUE SHOULD NOT DUCK, because it determines whether the issue is answerable in principle: WHAT WOULD THE RIGHT MEASUREMENT EVEN LOOK LIKE? Attribution is unlike the tasks calibration is normally measured on, because the ground truth is itself contested, aliased and sometimes genuinely underdetermined by the report -- which is precisely why CTIBench needed a 'plausible' bucket and why it scores an ALIAS as correct. A confidence measurement that ignored that would be measuring the wrong thing. So a well-posed target is narrower than 'is the model calibrated': it is whether a model's expressed confidence DISCRIMINATES between reports whose attribution is determined by the evidence and reports whose attribution is not. If no published work measures that, saying so with this reasoning attached is a legitimate resolution of this issue and should be recorded as such rather than treated as a failure to find an answer.

THE FINDING: NO SOURCE IN THIS KNOWLEDGE BASE MEASURES EXPRESSED CONFIDENCE ON THREAT-ACTOR ATTRIBUTION. src-0002 partitions outputs by correctness only -- its metric section defines accuracy for CTI-MCQ and CTI-RCM, MAD for CTI-VSP, F1 for CTI-ATE, and the three-bucket correct/plausible/incorrect partition for CTI-TAA, and nothing else -- so it records no verbalised confidence, no hedging rate, no calibration metric and no reader-facing plausibility judgement, and no sentence in the paper interprets the correct-versus-plausible gap. src-0007's 'Content: Threat Actor' block is an LLM-judged 1-5 quality rubric that grades attribution QUALITY rather than how confidently the model asserts it, and per ctr-0008 its 'Attribution' row measures SOURCE LINKING rather than actor identification. src-0004 is a single published passage with no measurement attached at all. issues.title: Is 'AI-generated CTI reliability' a single property, or does it vary sharply by task type (mechanical extraction vs. open-ended reasoning)?
open_questions: SPLIT NOTE (cycle 16, T2, discharging carry-forward [1] after it was carried unactioned for nine consecutive cycles). This issue now covers ONLY the narrow claim: that AI-generated CTI reliability varies sharply by sub-task rather than being a single uniform property. The SPECIFIC ORDINAL AXIS ('mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation'), together with the cycle-2 proposed cross-source synthesis that carried it and the open question about whether a better explanatory variable exists, was MOVED VERBATIM to the new issue 'extraction-vs-reasoning-ordinal-axis'. The reason for the split is that the two claims have very different evidential status and were sharing one issue and one candidate_resolution from cycle 2 to cycle 15, which is exactly why no T4 could score either honestly: the narrow claim has five independent supporting sources (src-0001, src-0002, src-0006, src-0007, and now src-0013 on the calibration axis) while the ordinal axis is actively disputed between src-0006 and src-0007. Do NOT re-merge them.

src-0006's causal-intervention mitigations raised an attribution-adjacent task (Threat Actor Linking) by only +0.055 accuracy, a much smaller gain than LANCE's ~72-86%->97.6% F1 jump on IoC extraction (src-0003) -- but the two are not a controlled comparison (different tasks, metrics, mitigation types: automated retrieval/inference intervention vs. human-in-the-loop regex+LLM pipeline). No source yet tests a LANCE-style human-validated pipeline specifically on ATT&CK mapping or attribution; a search this cycle for such a study (and for RAM/src-2502.02337, an automated non-human-in-the-loop ATT&CK mapper) found none. Does human-in-the-loop validation specifically (not just any targeted mitigation) transfer to reasoning-heavy tasks, and if so how much of the IoC-extraction gain would it recover?

Since src-0003's strong result is single-study/in-house, would the task-dependence conclusion survive an independent replication showing a smaller IoC-extraction advantage? A cycle-6 search for independent LANCE/PRISM replication or critique found none published yet.

candidate_resolutions.summary: The core, narrower claim -- that AI-generated CTI reliability is genuinely task-dependent rather than a single uniform property -- is now supported, not just proposed: src-0006 (cycle 6) directly measures reliability across multiple distinct CTI sub-tasks within one consistent study design (rather than only via cross-benchmark synthesis across different teams/models) and finds F1/AUC ranging roughly 0.20-0.90 by specific sub-task, corroborating the cross-study pattern already visible in src-0001/0002/0003/0005. However, the SPECIFIC ordinal axis proposed above (mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation) is not confirmed by this evidence and is likely too coarse: src-0006 found its failure patterns cut across all 4 CTI pipeline stages it defines, including extraction/contextualization-type tasks, rather than concentrating in 'reasoning' stages. So: task-dependence itself = supported; the specific extraction-vs-reasoning explanatory axis = open, and now positively questioned rather than merely unverified.

ADDED cycle 16 by T2 at the split. Two further within-study measurements strengthen the NARROW claim -- that CTI reliability varies sharply by sub-task rather than being one uniform property -- and both are of the strongest available kind, holding team, corpus, models and harness constant and varying only the sub-task. (1) src-0007: on one expert-annotated corpus drawn from a real company's CTI workflow, the same four models reach IoC-extraction precision 0.8240-0.8846 while scoring 0.2787/0.2270 (GPT-4o) and 0.3480/0.1759 (o3-mini) precision/recall on MITRE ATT&CK TTP identification, and GPT-4o scores 1.140 out of 5 on the threat-actor Attribution rubric against 3.612 out of 5 for root-cause content in the same table -- roughly a 3x spread across sub-tasks with everything else held constant. (2) src-0013 extends task-dependence to a NEW AXIS that no prior source in this base had tested: reliability varies by sub-task not only in accuracy but in CALIBRATION. SCOPE LIMIT ON (2), do not strip it: src-0013 measures secure code generation, not CTI, so it corroborates the SHAPE of task-dependence on a security-adjacent task rather than replicating it on CTI material -- see the cycle-16 scope ruling recorded in 'consistency-calibration-as-failure-mode', which declines to treat security-adjacent corroboration as CTI multi-source support. THE CLAIM: the proposed ordinal axis 'mechanical extraction < classification < attribution < generation' is NOT supported by the only commensurable cross-sub-task measurement available in this base, and the extraction-versus-reasoning binary is too coarse to explain where CTI reliability breaks down. TWO INDEPENDENT ROUTES, from two unaffiliated teams on two corpora with two disjoint model sets. (1) src-0006's Table 2 restricted to its nine F1 rows -- one corpus, one 15-model set, one metric -- gives a Contextualization stage mean of 0.636 (IOC Normalization 0.656, Affected Systems 0.650, Attack Infrastructure 0.631, Malware Family Mapping 0.607) against an Attribution stage mean of 0.602 (TTP Extraction 0.673, Infrastructure Reuse 0.612, Relation Graph Building 0.610, False Flag Detection 0.511). The 0.034 gap is in the predicted direction but is roughly one eighth of the 0.272 mean between-model spread on a single task, and the best task in the subset is an Attribution-stage task. (2) src-0007's Table 4, the source that appears to support the ordering, reverses its own middle-to-third rung between two models: GPT-4o's attribution rubric of 1.140/5 normalises to 0.228 or 0.035 against a derived TTP F1 of 0.2502 (at or below), while o3-mini's 2.968/5 normalises to 0.594 or 0.492 against 0.2337 (above), under both defensible normalisations. THREE MATERIAL CAVEATS. (a) src-0006 reports no confidence intervals, no seeds and no repeat runs, so 0.034 carries no uncertainty estimate; this candidate asserts that the ordering is NOT SUPPORTED, not that the reverse ordering holds. (b) Four of the nine rows are strictly monotone decreasing across all eight general-purpose columns in printed order, a pattern of unknown cause verified as-printed by three pulls across two URL forms; dropping all four leaves 0.641 against 0.592, gap 0.049, same direction, same best task. (c) The fourth rung of the proposed ordering, open-ended GENERATION, is not represented in the commensurable subset at all, so this candidate refutes the extraction-versus-classification-versus-attribution part of the ordering and is SILENT on generation, which remains supported in the parent issue by src-0001's extraction-versus-generation confidence-interval-width split of 0.02 against 0.06.

PROPOSED, entered cycle 18 as the replacement explanatory variable this issue's inherited first open_question asked for. THE CLAIM: model identity explains as much of the variance in CTI sub-task reliability as sub-task identity does, corpus identity may explain more than either, and the extraction-versus-reasoning category is a weak third. On src-0006's nine-row commensurable F1 subset the mean between-model range within a task is 0.272 and the mean between-task range within a model is 0.263 -- equal to within 0.009 -- while the extraction-versus-reasoning stage gap on those same rows is 0.034. Separately, the same nominal sub-task, ATT&CK TTP mapping, scores F1 0.478-0.751 in src-0006 against a derived F1 of 0.157-0.250 in src-0007: a shift of roughly 0.4 on one task, larger than any between-task gap either paper reports. THREE OBJECTIONS TO ITSELF, which is why this is proposed and not supported. (i) The between-model and between-task figures are RANGES, not variance components; a range is sensitive to a single outlying model, and src-0006's LLY is an outlier on two of the nine rows (False Flag Detection 0.286, Patch Recommendation 0.442). (ii) The cross-source TTP comparison is uncontrolled -- task definition, model set, publication year and metric decomposition all differ at once -- so corpus identity is only one of at least four candidate explanations for that 0.4 shift. (iii) Both figures come from ONE study's table, and no cycle has checked whether the same equality holds in any other multi-model multi-task security evaluation; src-0014's roughly fourfold spread in prompt-sensitivity between models on identical data introduces a fourth variable, prompt strategy, that this candidate does not account for at all.

issues.title: Have AI-generated CTI failures already reached production/publication at real institutions, and how do institutions respond when caught?
open_questions: REWRITTEN cycle 12, and deliberately reframed so it stops being answerable by anecdote. The base rate of hallucinated citations across CTI PUBLISHERS is still unmeasured and no cycle should claim otherwise: we now have two named incidents (ENISA src-0004, EY Canada src-0012), and two anecdotes are not a rate. What was found instead is the nearest systematic audit in an ADJACENT population -- src-0011 (GhostCite) manually verified 2.2M citations across 56,381 papers and reports 1.01% of papers at Security venues containing at least one invalid citation. It cannot be transferred to CTI: it audits peer-reviewed conference papers, defines a ghost citation as one absent from academic databases (inapplicable to CTI footnotes, which are news/vendor URLs), and reports per-PAPER rates that are not comparable with src-0004's per-FOOTNOTE 26/492. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE THIS: (a) a link-resolution/footnote-verification sweep over N published threat reports from M agencies and vendors, which is mechanically cheap since both known incidents were found precisely this way (dead links); (b) a disclosure-policy survey of CTI publishers; or (c) an existing audit of vendor/agency reports if one can be found. Cycle 12 searched for (c) and found only academic-corpus and consulting-report audits, never a CTI-publisher audit.

PARTIALLY ANSWERED cycle 12, first half CLOSED. ENISA's AI usage was NOT disclosed to readers before publication and was admitted only when Der Spiegel asked after external researchers found the dead links (src-0004). Stronger now: ENISA's own publication pages for BOTH affected reports (src-0009, src-0010) carry revision notices dated 09 January 2026 describing the fix purely mechanically -- 'updated to edit some links' and 'updated to correct some broken links and typos' -- and as of 2026-07-29, roughly 8 months after exposure, NEITHER page carries any mention of AI or generative AI. So the non-disclosure was not merely pre-publication; it persists in the corrected record. STILL OPEN: whether ENISA changed any internal policy (a cycle-12 search found no published policy change), and whether any peer agency changed disclosure policy in response. Also still open at PDF level: the front matter / legal notice of the v1.2 PDFs was not pulled, so the 'no AI disclosure anywhere' claim is currently established only for the landing pages.

PARTIALLY ANSWERED cycle 12, and the answer for the NUMBER is no. ENISA's own primary artefacts (src-0009, src-0010) independently corroborate the STRUCTURE of the incident -- two reports, published October 1 and November 6 2025, both revised on 09 January 2026, both revisions concerning links -- exactly as src-0004 reports secondhand. But neither ENISA page gives any footnote count and neither mentions AI, so the 26-of-492 figure remains sourced to Der Spiegel via Heise and is corroborated only by outlets (cybernews, Tagesspiegel, derStandard) that themselves cite Der Spiegel, i.e. NOT independently. NOTE FOR FUTURE CYCLES: Der Spiegel's original article could not be retrieved -- spiegel.de is blocked to this agent's user agent (WebSearch returns HTTP 400 'domains are not accessible to our user agent'), so this is an infrastructure limit, not an unsearched direction; do not burn budget retrying it the same way. The remaining routes to the number are counting the footnotes in the archived v1.1/original PDF against v1.2, or locating Prof. Christian Dietrich's / Institut fuer Internet-Sicherheit's own writeup. ENISA's silence is NOT a contradiction of src-0004 and no G3 entry was opened: the notices assign no cause at all rather than a competing one.

NEW cycle 12. Institutional responses to the SAME failure mode diverged sharply -- EY Canada withdrew the offending report entirely and issued a statement invoking its 'organisation-wide commitment to the responsible use of AI' (src-0012), while ENISA retained both reports, patched the links, and described the correction without reference to AI (src-0009, src-0010). What predicts which response an institution gives: commercial reputational exposure vs public-mandate insulation, the presence of a named external investigator, the share of citations affected (16/27 = 59% for EY vs 26/492 = 5% for ENISA), or something else? Two cases cannot distinguish these; more incidents with recorded responses would.

NEW cycle 12. BOTH known incidents were discovered from the outside by parties clicking through footnotes (Westfaelische Hochschule researchers for ENISA, GPTZero for EY), and in neither case did the publisher's internal QA catch it. src-0011 supplies a measured analogue of why in academic publishing (76.7% of surveyed reviewers do not thoroughly check references; 80.0% never suspect fake citations). Does ANY CTI publisher run automated link-resolution or citation-verification on reports before release, and is there a single documented case of this failure mode being caught internally? No source in the base documents one.

candidate_resolutions.summary: At least one major institutional CTI publisher (ENISA, the EU's cybersecurity agency) published AI-hallucinated citations in production threat-landscape reports (Oct/Nov 2025), including a technical fingerprint (misattributing the name 'APT29' to Microsoft's naming convention, when Microsoft actually uses 'Midnight Blizzard') consistent with LLM-generated text. The failure was caught by external academic researchers checking footnote links, not by internal QA, and the agency's public response ('human errors') did not fully acknowledge AI attribution even after exposure. This establishes existence of the failure mode in production but not its frequency/base rate across the CTI industry.

ADDED cycle 12. The ENISA incident is no longer carried by a single secondary source. ENISA's own publication pages for both named reports independently corroborate the incident's verifiable structure: 'ENISA Threat Landscape 2025' (published 1 Oct 2025) carries 'Revision Notice - Version 1.2. (09 January 2026): This publication has been updated to edit some links.' and the sectorial 'Public Administration' report (published 6 Nov 2025) carries 'Revision Notice - Version 1.2 (09 January 2026): This publication has been updated to correct some broken links and typos.' Two reports, October and November 2025, both corrected for links on the same January 2026 date -- matching src-0004's secondhand account on report count, dates and defect type. What ENISA's own record does NOT contain is any footnote count and any mention of AI, so the 26/492 figure and the AI attribution remain dependent on Der Spiegel via Heise.

ADDED cycle 12. The failure mode RECURS across institution types and is not an ENISA idiosyncrasy. EY Canada's 2025 report 'Points of Attack: Uncovering Cyber Threats and Fraud in Loyalty Systems' was found by GPTZero (14 May 2026) to have 16 of 27 references hallucinated, with 'more than a half-dozen footnotes led to dead webpages or did not contain the cited information'; EY Canada removed the study from its website. This is a commercial Big Four publisher of security/fraud content, discovered by the same route as ENISA (an outside party clicking through footnotes) roughly six months later. Two independent institutions, one public and one commercial, is materially stronger than one for the EXISTENCE and RECURRENCE claim -- and still says nothing about frequency. Scope note: loyalty-systems fraud is security-adjacent published content, not threat intelligence in the narrow IoC/TTP/attribution sense measured elsewhere in this knowledge base.

ADDED cycle 12. On the issue's second question -- how institutions respond when caught -- the two documented cases diverge, so there is no single institutional response pattern to report. EY Canada WITHDREW the report and issued a statement referencing accuracy and 'an organisation-wide commitment to the responsible use of AI', saying it was reviewing why the study was published. ENISA RETAINED both reports, issued v1.2 corrections describing only link edits and typos, characterised the underlying errors to the press as 'human errors' while confirming AI was permitted for 'minor editorial revisions', and as of 2026-07-29 carries no AI disclosure on either publication page. The common element across both is that neither institution's internal QA detected the problem and both were corrected only after external publication of the finding.

ADDED cycle 12, status PROPOSED and deliberately not promoted -- read the scope limit before citing. No base rate for hallucinated citations in CTI publications exists. The closest systematic measurement is src-0011 (GhostCite), which manually verified a flagged subset of 2.2M citations across 56,381 papers at top AI/ML and Security venues (2020-2025) and found 1.07% of papers overall, and 1.01% of papers at Security venues, containing at least one invalid or fabricated citation, with an 80.9% increase in 2025 alone and the authors calling their figure 'a conservative lower bound'. This is NOT the CTI rate and must not be quoted as one: different population (peer-reviewed conference papers, which have reviewers; CTI reports have none), different citation ecology (academic references vs news/vendor URLs), and different denominator (per-paper vs src-0004's per-footnote 26/492). What it does support is a directional claim -- that fabricated citations survive into refereed security literature at a nonzero and rising rate despite peer review -- which makes it implausible that unrefereed CTI publishing is cleaner. That inference is the proposed part, and no source tests it.

issues.title: Do LLM-based security triage and response systems fail by accepting or acting on far too much -- an under-refusal failure that accuracy-based evaluation does not detect?
open_questions: IS OVER-ACCEPTANCE A PROPERTY OF THE MODELS OR OF THE HARNESS? This is the issue's central unknown and neither source addresses it. Neither src-0007 nor src-0015 varies the decision threshold, the stated cost of a false positive in the prompt, the availability of an explicit abstain option, or the presence of a human confirmation step. src-0003 established for a different sub-task (IoC extraction) that scaffolding around the model can dominate measured reliability; the analogous experiment for triage -- does an explicit abstain option, a stated false-positive cost, or a required evidence-fetch step move precision (Accepted) off 0.27-0.40 -- has not been run by any source in this base. Until it is, 'the models under-refuse' and 'these harnesses were built with no refusal affordance' are indistinguishable.

WHAT IS THE OPERATIONAL COST, and is it actually worse than the status quo? Neither source converts its false-positive rate into analyst hours, containment blast radius, or alert-fatigue effects, so precision (Accepted) of 0.27 cannot yet be compared against human triage on any common currency. Note a structural obstacle: src-0007's ground truth IS the human analyst's accept/reject decision, so by construction it carries no human error bar and cannot tell us whether human triage would score better on its own benchmark.

MERGED IN FROM carry-forward [15] at the cycle-16 split decision; cycle 12 excluded this from the knowledge base as a source and cycle 16 judges it belongs HERE, as an open question rather than as evidence. The mirror image of automated over-acceptance is AI-generated security claims arriving INBOUND in volume: curl ended its HackerOne bug bounty on 31 January 2026 after a flood of AI-generated 'slop' vulnerability reports, with reported figures of roughly 20% of submissions being AI slop by mid-2025 and the confirmed-vulnerability rate falling from about 15% historically to under 5%. 'AI slop arrives inbound AND automated triage cannot filter it' is a coherent single problem that this issue and carry-forward [15] describe better jointly than either does alone -- and it has a sharp practical edge, because if automated triage accepts 60-73% of what human analysts reject, it is precisely the wrong instrument for the volume problem it is most often proposed to solve. THIS IS NOT YET EVIDENCE AND MUST NOT BE CITED AS SUCH: no curl/HackerOne source exists in state/knowledge/index.json and a T2 must not invent sources (G1). A future T1 should collect it, reported at bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/curl-ending-bug-bounty-program-after-flood-of-ai-slop-reports/. Until collected, this is a question, not a claim.

Does the under-refusal generalise to the CTI sub-tasks measured elsewhere in this base? If a model were asked to extract IoCs or map ATT&CK techniques with an explicit 'insufficient evidence' option available, would it use it? src-0014 supplies this base's only abstention data -- self-consistency collapsing coverage to 24.04-60.85% -- but on vulnerability detection rather than CTI, and it measures abstention INDUCED by sampling disagreement rather than abstention OFFERED as a choice, so it does not answer this.

Is there a trade-off frontier, or is this simply a badly-set threshold? src-0007's recall (Accepted) of 0.90-1.00 alongside precision of 0.27-0.40 is consistent with a threshold set to maximise recall; nobody has published the precision the same models reach at a recall of, say, 0.7. If the frontier is favourable, this is a tuning problem and largely solved; if precision stays low across the whole frontier, it is a capability problem. No source in this base reports a precision-recall curve for triage.

candidate_resolutions.summary: CREATED cycle 16 by T2, discharging carry-forward [3] and merging carry-forward [15]; six cycles elapsed between the first proposal of this issue and the first cycle with standing to create it. Two independent sources -- different teams, different task framings, different model generations, different years -- find the same failure: the decision threshold is set so permissively that the system accepts or acts on most of what a human analyst would reject. src-0007 (CyberThreat-Eval; Microsoft Research/Microsoft/HKUST, Mar 2026) measures automated triage on a real company's daily CTI workflow and reports an extreme asymmetry, recall (Accepted) 0.90-1.00 against precision (Accepted) 0.27-0.40 across all four models tested. src-0015 (OpenSec, Jan 2026) measures frontier incident-response agents over 40 episodes per model and finds GPT-5.2 containing in 100% of episodes at an 82.5% false-positive rate, DeepSeek 3.2 92.5% at 65%, Gemini 3 75% at 57.5%, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 62.5% at 45%, with an evidence-gated action rate of only 0.375-0.542 -- every model acts without first fetching trusted evidence about the target entity on a majority or near-majority of its containment actions. WHY THIS IS AN ISSUE AND NOT A FOOTNOTE UNDER ACCURACY: src-0015 locates the defect precisely, stating that 'All models correctly identify the ground-truth threat when they act; the calibration gap is not in detection but in restraint.' Detection accuracy is fine. These systems would be scored WELL by essentially every metric used elsewhere in this knowledge base, and the defect is invisible to all of them -- which is exactly the argument for giving it its own issue rather than filing it under an existing accuracy-shaped one. PROVENANCE ASYMMETRY, do not flatten it: src-0007 is institutionally affiliated, methodologically detailed, and had all nine of its stored Table 4 rows re-verified verbatim by cycle 15's G2 exact to four decimal places; src-0015 is by its own recorded assessment the weakest-provenance source in this base -- single-author preprint filed cs.AI, no stated venue, peer review or affiliation, n=40 synthetic RL-seed episodes per model with no confidence intervals, and only the GPT-5.2-versus-Sonnet-4.5 contrast robust, with the middle two models' ordering unresolved. The claim therefore RESTS on src-0007; src-0015 corroborates its direction on a different task and a newer model generation, which is worth a great deal for showing the failure is not one benchmark's artefact, and is worth little as independent quantification. ONE POOLING ERROR TO AVOID: src-0015's 'calibration' is an action-threshold construct (false-positive rate, evidence-gating), NOT the ECE/Brier confidence calibration of src-0001 and src-0013, and the two must never be averaged or quoted as the same measurement.

contradictions.description: ONE ISSUE ASSERTS AS SUPPORTED EXACTLY WHAT ANOTHER ISSUE HAS FORMALLY WITHDRAWN, ON THE SAME TABLE AND THE SAME NUMBERS. Opened by the cycle-33 T4 while pricing carry-forward [47](d) and [34]. This is a conflict between two SUPPORTED claims inside this state, which is precisely G3's test, and it is filed nowhere else: ctr-0008 covers only the 1.140-versus-3.612 half and is filed against a DIFFERENT issue_id, and ctr-0004 is filed against ioc-extraction-reliability. NO contradiction entry has ever been filed against task-dependent-reliability-framing. THE CLAIM IN CONFLICT, verbatim from this issue's SECOND candidate_resolution (status 'supported', evidence [src-0007, src-0013], added cycle 16 by T2): 'Two further within-study measurements strengthen the NARROW claim -- that CTI reliability varies sharply by sub-task rather than being one uniform property -- and both are of the strongest available kind, holding team, corpus, models and harness constant and varying only the sub-task. (1) src-0007: on one expert-annotated corpus drawn from a real company's CTI workflow, the same four models reach IoC-extraction precision 0.8240-0.8846 while scoring 0.2787/0.2270 (GPT-4o) and 0.3480/0.1759 (o3-mini) precision/recall on MITRE ATT&CK TTP identification, and GPT-4o scores 1.140 out of 5 on the threat-actor Attribution rubric against 3.612 out of 5 for root-cause content in the same table -- roughly a 3x spread across sub-tasks with everything else held constant.' BOTH OF ITS TWO src-0007 COMPARISONS ARE NOW KNOWN TO BE NON-COMMENSURABLE, EACH REFUTED BY A SUPPORTED CANDIDATE ELSEWHERE IN THIS GRAPH, AND ITS STATED METHODOLOGICAL WARRANT IS FALSE. CONFLICT 1 -- THE IoC-VERSUS-TTP SPREAD. ttp-attack-mapping-reliability's candidate 2 carries a cycle-31 addendum headed 'CLAIM (b) IS NOW WITHDRAWN' which withdraws THIS EXACT INFERENCE in this exact form: 'The argument was that because the identical models on the identical corpus through the identical harness reach 0.8240-0.8846 precision on mechanical IoC extraction in the same table, the ATT&CK deficit cannot be attributed to corpus difficulty or prompt harness quality. That inference silently assumed the two numbers were produced by comparable scoring. THEY ARE NOT.' The two rules are now BOTH known from executing code in one artefact (src-0017): the IoC side is ONE-DIRECTIONAL SUBSTRING CONTAINMENT, any(pred.lower() in gt.lower() for gt in gt_set) (ctr-0004, cycle 27), and the ATT&CK side is EXACT TECHNIQUE-ID SET INTERSECTION with no substring, parent, sub-technique or partial credit (ttp candidate 3, read cycle 31 and REPLICATED cycle 32 with ten verbatim string checks, plus the finding that TTP_Mapping.csv carries a 'sub-technique of' parent column WHICH THE LOADER DISCARDS, so a T1548.002 prediction against a T1548 ground truth is counted as a false positive AND a false negative simultaneously). THE DECISIVE POINT, AND IT IS NEW HERE RATHER THAN INHERITED: THE DIRECTION OF THE SCORING BIAS IS THE DIRECTION OF THE REPORTED FINDING. The leniently-scored task is the one that scores high and the strictly-scored task is the one that scores low. So the 3x spread this candidate presents as a sub-task difficulty fact is exactly what these two scoring rules would manufacture from equal underlying performance. The confound is no longer merely possible and unquantified; its SIGN is known and it aligns with the claim. CONFLICT 2 -- THE 1.140-VERSUS-3.612 RUBRIC CONTRAST. Per ctr-0008 (cycle 30, confirmed by two fetches of the paper's Appendix C.2 on two URL renderings and again at cycle 31 from the live sys_prompt string in eval/root_cause.py retrieved whole), the dimension named 'Attribution' IS DEFINED DIFFERENTLY IN THE TWO RUBRIC BLOCKS: in the Threat Actor block it measures SOURCE LINKING ('5: Fully attributable; all details are clearly linked to the original article'), and no anchor in that block mentions identifying a threat actor; in the Root Cause block it measures THREAT-ACTOR IDENTIFICATION ('5: Perfect attribution; accurately identifies the threat actor, their objectives, and the precise relationship to the incident's root cause'). 1.140 and 3.612 are two different constructs sharing one column name, and the labels run OPPOSITE to the way this candidate reads them. WHY THIS IS FILED AGAINST THIS ISSUE AND NOT LEFT TO ctr-0008. ctr-0008 flags this issue in passing as having 'the LARGEST SCORING EXPOSURE' but is filed against attribution-confident-wrong-gap, so per-issue queries over open contradictions do not surface it here, and it does not address conflict 1 at all. Conflict 1 is unfiled anywhere against this issue. THE FALSE WARRANT, WHICH IS THE MOST TRANSFERABLE PART. The candidate's own justification for treating these as strong evidence is that they are 'of the strongest available kind, holding team, corpus, models and harness constant and varying only the sub-task'. That is carry-forward [34] stated as a virtue and it is false: A WITHIN-STUDY DESIGN DOES NOT HOLD THE SCORING RULE CONSTANT, and both of this candidate's within-study comparisons are now demonstrated instances of the rule varying with the sub-task. There are now SEVEN documented non-commensurable instances in this base (src-0017/ctr-0004; src-0003's classification-over-a-regex-candidate-set; src-0005's all-or-nothing multi-select; src-0002/ctr-0006's Micro-versus-Macro-F1 with no stated ATT&CK correctness rule; src-0007's rubric against itself per ctr-0008; src-0007's IoC rule against its own ATT&CK rule; and src-0008's body text against its own Table 6 caption). EVERY TIME A CYCLE HAS ACTUALLY READ A SCORING RULE IN THIS BASE, IT HAS DIFFERED FROM WHAT THE STATE ASSUMED. That is now the base rate and it must be the prior. NEITHER SIDE IS SILENTLY PICKED, AND WHAT SURVIVES IS STATED SO THE REPAIR IS NOT OVER-READ AS A DEMOLITION. (a) src-0013's leg of this same candidate is untouched by anything here and is not in dispute. (b) The BLOCK-LEVEL rubric contrast survives conflict 2 and is broader than the sentence it would replace: GPT-4o scores 1.547 / 1.528 / 1.145 / 2.019 / 1.734 / 1.140 on Threat Actor content against 3.686 / 3.458 / 3.362 / 3.932 / 3.753 / 3.612 on Root Cause content, LOWER ON ALL SIX DIMENSIONS. But ctr-0008 records two limits on even that, and they apply here with full force: the two blocks' anchors are worded differently, so it remains a contrast between two differently-worded rubrics over two different sub-tasks, and the instrument is an LLM judge which the paper states is GPT-4o, one of the four models being scored. (c) The QUALITATIVE direction -- that measured CTI reliability is not one uniform property -- is NOT refuted by this entry and is separately carried by this issue's FIRST candidate via src-0006. THIS ENTRY DISPUTES THE WITHIN-STUDY COMPARISONS OFFERED AS THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE, NOT THE ISSUE'S EXISTENCE. RESOLUTION PATH, FOR A T3 TARGETING THIS ISSUE. (i) Rewrite candidate 2 to drop the words 'varying only the sub-task' and to state the scoring-rule objection explicitly, replacing the IoC-versus-TTP sentence with the qualitative statement that the two figures are scored by different KINDS of matching whose bias runs in the direction of the observed gap, and replacing the 1.140-versus-3.612 sentence with the six-dimension block contrast plus its two limits. (ii) STATE AND ANSWER THE OBJECTION IN THE ISSUE TEXT, which is what cycle 22 asked for and no cycle has done -- an issue cannot be credited with addressing a counterargument it has not noticed. (iii) Pull src-0006's per-task scoring definitions, which no cycle has ever read: candidate 1 and route 1 of extraction-vs-reasoning-ordinal-axis BOTH rest on the assumption that its nine F1 rows share one matching rule, and given the base rate above that assumption is now the single largest untested load-bearing assumption in this project. If those rules turn out comparable, this issue's level-3 case is repairable and cycle 19's argument stands as written.

METRIC-DEFINITION CONFLICT INSIDE A SINGLE TABLE, opened by cycle 30's G2 re-verification of src-0007 (arXiv 2603.09452, CyberThreat-Eval, Microsoft Research / Microsoft / HKUST). Target chosen by staleness: the Table 4 rubric rows were a single unreplicated pull from cycle 15, and that gap is the stated reason this issue's THIRD candidate_resolution is still 'proposed'. THE NUMBERS PASS COMPLETELY AND MUST NOT BE RE-OPENED. A third independent pull of arxiv.org/html/2603.09452v1, instructed to transcribe Table 4 whole and to write CANNOT READ rather than infer, returned every one of its 34 data rows identical to the transcription stored in state/knowledge/src-0007.md, cell for cell -- including every rubric cell this issue cites: Content: Threat Actor GPT-4o 1.547 / 1.528 / 1.145 / 2.019 / 1.734 / 1.140 against o3-mini 3.964 / 3.656 / 3.165 / 4.753 / 4.731 / 2.968, and Content: Root Cause GPT-4o 3.686 / 3.458 / 3.362 / 3.932 / 3.753 / 3.612. The GPT-4o (FT) anomaly of carry-forward [19] is REPRODUCED A THIRD TIME (3.964 / 3.655 / 3.165 / 4.752 / 4.731 / 2.967, tracking o3-mini to within 0.001 on all six rubric rows) -- as-printed across three pulls at cycles 15, 21 and 30, cause still unknown, DO NOT GUESS. THE DEFECT IS IN OUR READING OF THE ROW, NOT IN THE ROW: this is methodological rule (vi), a clean source with an unclean state account of it, and it was caught by rule (iii), pulling the verbatim DEFINITION of the metric rather than only its value. WHAT THE SOURCE ACTUALLY DEFINES. Appendix C.2 prints SEPARATE criteria blocks for Threat Actor content and Root Cause content, and the dimension named 'Attribution' IS DEFINED DIFFERENTLY IN THE TWO BLOCKS. Verbatim, THREAT ACTOR block, all five anchors: 'Attribution: 1: Information is unverified or unattributed. 2: Major attribution issues; many details are not clearly linked. 3: Moderately attributable; some details lack clear source references. 4: Mostly attributable; minor gaps in linking information. 5: Fully attributable; all details are clearly linked to the original article.' Verbatim, ROOT CAUSE block, all five anchors: 'Attribution: 1: Completely incorrect attribution. 2: Significant attribution errors; misidentified threat actor. 3: Basic attribution; minor inaccuracies. 4: Mostly correct attribution. 5: Perfect attribution; clearly identifies the threat actor.' So in the Threat Actor block 'Attribution' measures SOURCE LINKING -- whether the generated text is traceable to the input article -- and NO anchor in that block mentions identifying a threat actor. In the Root Cause block 'Attribution' measures THREAT-ACTOR IDENTIFICATION and says so in three of its five anchors. Confirmed by two fetches on two URL renderings (arxiv.org/html/2603.09452v1 and arxiv.org/html/2603.09452), the second asked for both blocks whole with every numbered anchor and permitted to answer ABSENT or CANNOT READ. A one-sentence gloss from the first fetch, 'Attribution: Evaluates whether the generated context properly attributes information to the original article', is consistent with the fuller anchors. THE CLAIM IN CONFLICT, verbatim from this issue's third candidate_resolution: 'THE LOAD-BEARING PART IS THE WITHIN-TABLE CONTRAST, not the model gap: the same GPT-4o scores 3.686 / 3.458 / 3.612 on Content: Root Cause in the same table, so its 1.140 on threat-actor attribution is a deficit specific to attribution rather than a general inability to draft.' That contrast sets 1.140 against 3.612, and those two cells are NOT the same measurement.
